content: If you are allergic to quinine, quinidine, or mefloquine, or if you have any other allergies, inform your doctor or pharmacist before taking this medication. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could trigger allergic reactions or other complications. Quinine may cause dizziness or blurred vision. Consuming alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate these effects. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or engaging in activities that require alertness or clear vision until you are confident you can do so safely. Limit your intake of alcoholic beverages. This medication may lead to a condition affecting heart rhythm known as QT prolongation. The risk of QT prolongation increases if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also heighten this risk. This may occur if you are using certain medications, such as diuretics (water pills), or if you experience conditions like severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when absolutely necessary. Discuss the potential risks, benefits, and treatment options with your doctor. Quinine passes into breast milk, but it is unlikely to harm most nursing infants. However, your doctor may test your infant for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency before you breastfeed. Drug interactions can alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. This document does not list all possible drug interactions. Maintain a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Other medications may affect the removal of quinine from your body, potentially altering its effectiveness. Similarly, quinine can slow the removal of other drugs from your body, which may affect how they work. Many drugs, in addition to quinine, can affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation). Examples include amiodarone, dofetilide, mefloquine, pimozide, procainamide, quinidine, sotalol, and macrolide antibiotics (such as erythromycin), among others. Quinine is very similar to quinidine. This medication may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as urine tests for catecholamines, protein, or steroids, potentially causing false results. Inform laboratory personnel and your doctors that you are using this drug. In the event of an overdose, if someone exhibits serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. Laboratory and/or medical tests (such as G6PD blood levels, vision tests, blood potassium levels, liver/kidney function tests, and EKG) may be conducted while you are taking this medication. Ensure you attend all medical and laboratory appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is more than 4 hours after the missed dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that this product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warns that quinine should not be used to treat leg cramps, as it has not been proven effective for this purpose and may cause serious side effects. This medication is used alone or with other medications to treat malaria caused by mosquito bites in regions where malaria is common. Malaria parasites enter the body through mosquito bites and reside in tissues such as red blood cells or the liver. This medication targets and kills malaria parasites living inside red blood cells. In some cases, another medication (such as primaquine) may be required to eliminate parasites in other tissues. Both drugs may be necessary for a complete cure and to prevent relapse. Quinine belongs to a class of drugs known as antimalarials. The United States Centers for Disease Control (CDC) provides updated guidelines and travel recommendations for malaria prevention and treatment worldwide. Before starting quinine, read the Medication Guide and, if available, the Patient Information Leaflet provided by your pharmacist. Take this medication 2 to 3 hours before or after taking antacids containing aluminum or magnesium. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition, the country where you were infected, other medications you may be taking for malaria, and your response to treatment. It is crucial to take this medication (and other malaria medications) exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Do not take more or less of this drug than prescribed. Do not skip doses. Continue taking this medication until the full prescribed amount is finished, even if symptoms disappear after a few days. This medication works best when the drug level in your body is kept constant. Take it at evenly spaced intervals. Notify your doctor if you do not start feeling better after 1 to 2 days of starting this medication. Mild side effects may include headache, flushing, unusual sweating, nausea, ringing in the ears, decreased hearing, dizziness, blurred vision, and temporary changes in color vision. Quinine may also cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), especially during pregnancy. Symptoms of low blood sugar include sudden sweating, shaking, rapid heartbeat, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in the hands or feet. If these symptoms occur, raise your blood sugar by consuming a quick source of sugar, such as sugar, honey, candy, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Remember, this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefit to you outweighs the risk of side effects. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
